This can be false when a mod is experimental, in a deleted state or has only alpha files"*), `thumbsUpCount`, `rating` (nullable decimal).

`File` object: `id`, `gameId`, `modId`, `isAvailable` (*"Whether the file is available to download"*), `displayName`, `fileName`, `releaseType`, `fileStatus`, `hashes[]` (md5/sha1), `fileDate`, `fileLength`, `downloadCount`, `fileSizeOnDisk`, **`downloadUrl`** (*"The file download URL"*), `gameVersions[]`, `sortableGameVersions[]`, `dependencies[]` (`modId` + `relationType`), `exposeAsAlternative`, `parentProjectFileId`, `alternateFileId`, **`isServerPack`**, **`serverPackFileId`**, `isEarlyAccessContent`, `earlyAccessEndDate`, `fileFingerprint`, `modules[]`.

> `isServerPack` / `serverPackFileId` are the two fields that matter most for a hosting installer — many Minecraft modpacks ship a distinct server-side pack file.

### License: confirmed — **the CurseForge API does NOT expose a license field.** ✅

I grepped the entire rendered docs page (211 KB of text, every schema and every example response). The word "license" appears exactly **4 times**, all inside the *CurseForge for Studios Terms of Use* legal boilerplate ("non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide license to the name, logo and trademarks…"). It appears in **zero** schema definitions. There is no `license`, `licenseType`, `licenseUrl`, or `licenseName` on `Mod`, `File`, or any other object.

Corroborating evidence: [cfwidget.com](https://cfwidget.com/), the long-standing third-party CurseForge proxy, still has a `license` key in its JSON but it is **empty for every project I tested** — JEI, JourneyMap, Applied Energistics 2, Iron Chests, Create all return `"license": ""` (tested live against `api.cfwidget.com`).

**Where license lives instead:** on the CurseForge *website*, on the project's **License tab** (author-editable) and rendered in the project page's About panel. The support article on the distribution toggle says, verbatim: *"Simply click the 'Go to License Tab' button and you'll be transferred to the relevant tab… You can also edit this toggle by entering the project page > 'License tab'."* and *"Only project owners and members with the 'license' permission enabled can view the License tab"* ([Project Distribution Toggle](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000207877-project-distribution-toggle)).

**Practical consequence for you:** you cannot build a license-filtered catalog from the API. Getting license text means scraping `www.curseforge.com` — which is **explicitly prohibited** (see (g)) and technically blocked (I got `HTTP 403 "Just a moment… Enable JavaScript and cookies to continue"` — Cloudflare challenge — on both `curseforge.com/legal/terms` and `curseforge.com/terms/mod-author` from this server).

## (d) The `allowModDistribution=false` / `downloadUrl=null` problem

**What it is.** Authors can flip a per-project switch. Verbatim from CurseForge ([Project Distribution Toggle](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000207877-project-distribution-toggle)):

> "The project distribution toggle is all about providing authors control over their intellectual property and revenue generated from their awesome creations. The toggle is part of the new CurseForge API, and determines if 3rd party developers can or cannot distribute your project information and files."
>
> "If you turn this option off **Any 3rd-party service, website or client will not have access to your projects or files via the 3rd-party API.**"
>
> "If you turn this option on any download from the 3rd party service **will not count towards your total downloads nor towards your Reward Program earnings.**"
>
> "As a default, all existing projects have the option toggled on and allow distribution."
>
> **"We recommend choosing a license preference that is compatible with your distribution choice. In any case - the API will respect the toggle choice over the license type choice."**

That last sentence is the one to internalise: **an MIT- or LGPL-licensed mod can still have `allowModDistribution=false`, and CurseForge will enforce the toggle over the licence.** The open licence may give you the legal right to redistribute, but CurseForge will not serve you the bytes through the API.

**Mechanically**, `Mod.allowModDistribution=false` ⇒ `File.downloadUrl` comes back `null` and `/download-url` fails. The API returns full metadata but no file.

**How widespread?** No official statistic exists — I searched and could not find one, and CurseForge has never published a number. Only anecdotes, and they cut both ways:
- All the Mods 9 (a ~400-mod pack): 3 mods blocked.
- A 114-mod pack: 4 blocked ([xenodeve/minecraft-100day#80](https://github.com/xenodeve/minecraft-100day/issues/80)).
- Individual high-traffic libraries have been the pain point — e.g. long-running author requests on [architectury/architectury-api#262](https://github.com/architectury/architectury-api/issues/262), [EccentricVamp/EccentricTome#18](https://github.com/EccentricVamp/EccentricTome/issues/18), [Flemmli97/TenshiLib#8](https://github.com/Flemmli97/TenshiLib/issues/8), [mrsterner/GuardVillagers#23](https://github.com/mrsterner/GuardVillagers/issues/23), [r8420/MoreOverlays-updated#62](https://github.com/r8420/MoreOverlays-updated/issues/62).

**Realistic read: low single-digit percent of projects, but non-uniformly distributed** — it clusters on libraries and popular mods, so the probability that *a given modpack* contains at least one blocked mod is high. For your use case that is what matters: a 1–3% per-mod block rate is a ~50%+ per-pack failure rate.

**What third-party launchers actually do — they all give up and hand it to the human:**
- **Prism Launcher**: on a blocked mod the pack install halts and the user is given a link list; Prism then watches the Downloads folder and copies files into place. Tracked as bugs because the UX is bad: [#599 "Attempting to download mods from CurseForge that have 3rd party downloads disabled results in undetermined behavior"](https://github.com/PrismLauncher/PrismLauncher/issues/599) (version dropdown shows *"No valid version found!"*; downloads fail silently and the mod appears installed but isn't), [#3220](https://github.com/PrismLauncher/PrismLauncher/issues/3220), [#3844](https://github.com/PrismLauncher/PrismLauncher/issues/3844).
- **itzg/docker-minecraft-server** (the de-facto standard Minecraft server image, i.e. your closest analogue): verbatim from its docs — *"For mod, modpacks, and world files that are not allowed for automated download, the container path `/downloads` can be attached and matching files will be retrieved from there."* and *"It's important to use a browser to download the files listed for manual download."* ([auto-curseforge docs](https://docker-minecraft-server.readthedocs.io/en/latest/types-and-platforms/mod-platforms/auto-curseforge/))
- **Modrinth** deliberately does not integrate: *"some of them, like CurseForge, are Modrinth's competitors. They won't allow the use of their APIs to Modrinth, or if they do, it would be under a contract with terms that might make experience worse for Modrinth users."* ([modrinth/code#3631](https://github.com/modrinth/code/issues/3631))

**What it means for a hosting company.** You cannot promise "one-click install for any CurseForge mod." You must:
1. Store `allowModDistribution` per mod, refresh it (authors flip it), and **exclude or clearly badge blocked mods in your catalog UI** rather than failing at install time.
2. Provide an upload/SFTP fallback path for blocked mods — that is what every serious tool does, and it is also the honest answer to give customers.
3. Never construct a CDN URL to bypass the flag. Doing so circumvents an access-control mechanism, which is a named prohibited act in the API terms (see (g)) and voids the author consent that CurseForge's whole approval process is built around.

**Historical context**: the toggle shipped alongside the official API on 16 May 2022, which broke MultiMC/PolyMC/GDLauncher/PCL2 modpack installs. CurseForge's rationale, as reported: downloads from 3rd-party services rely on CurseForge servers and CDN, incurring costs and bypassing the monetization that funds the Author Rewards program.

## (e) CDN URL pattern, manual construction, and your 403 — **I reproduced this live**

### The URL scheme (empirically verified today from this server)

`edge.forgecdn.net` is a CloudFront distribution that **302-redirects** to `mediafilez.forgecdn.net` (Fastly/ioRiver in front of an S3 bucket). Observed:

```
GET https://edge.forgecdn.net/files/8911/160/jei-26.3-neoforge-31.0.0.7.jar
→ HTTP/2 302, location: https://mediafilez.forgecdn.net/files/8911/160/...
   (via CloudFront, x-amz-cf-pop: SIN3-P4)
→ HTTP/2 200, 1,905,807 bytes, content-type: application/java-archive
   (server: AmazonS3, x-ioriver: Fastly)
```

**The exact fileId → path rule (I tested all four variants):**

```
https://mediafilez.forgecdn.net/files/{floor(fileId/1000)}/{fileId % 1000}/{fileName}
```

| Tested path | Result |
|---|---|
| `/files/8911/160/jei-26.3-neoforge-31.0.0.7.jar` (id 8911160) | **200**, 1905807 B |
| `/files/8880/75/jei-26.2-neoforge-30.32.0.220.jar` (id 8880**075**) | **200**, 1919971 B |
| `/files/8880/**075**/…` (zero-padded) | **403** |
| `/files/8851/9/jei-1.20.1-forge-15.59.0.210.jar` (id 8851**009**) | **200**, 1825651 B |
| `/files/8851/**009**/…` (zero-padded) | **403** |

⚠️ **The second segment is NOT zero-padded.** This is the classic bug: fileId `8851009` → `8851/9`, not `8851/009`. Padding gives a 403. (Note the community shorthand *"the file id is segmented every four digits"* from [Coadon/CurseFetch](https://github.com/Coadon/CurseFetch) is a rough approximation that breaks on these cases — use `divmod(fileId, 1000)`.)

### Your 403 with empty body — diagnosed

**It is almost certainly `api.curseforge.com`, not the CDN.** I reproduced it exactly:

```
$ curl -D - https://api.curseforge.com/v1/games            # no key
HTTP/2 403
content-length: 0
x-cache: Error from cloudfront

$ curl -H "x-api-key: notarealkey" https://api.curseforge.com/v1/games
HTTP/2 403   (empty body)
```

**403 + `content-length: 0` + `x-cache: Error from cloudfront` is CloudFront rejecting the API key at the edge before your request reaches the app.** Causes, in order of likelihood:

1. **Key mangled by shell/env interpolation.** CurseForge keys are bcrypt-shaped (`$2a$10$…`). `$2a`, `$10` get eaten by shell `$`-expansion / Docker Compose variable substitution, silently truncating the key. This is by far the most-reported cause: [itzg/docker-minecraft-server#3591 "Access to CurseForge API is forbidden despite valid CF_API_KEY"](https://github.com/itzg/docker-minecraft-server/issues/3591) — the fix is no quotes in `.env`, or `$$` doubling in Compose. Check the key's exact byte length at the point of use.
2. **Key not authorised for that game.** Docs: *"Get all games that are available to the provided API key."* Keys are scoped; a Studios/game-developer key will 403 on Minecraft data.
3. **Rate limited.** When throttled, CloudFront returns a **403 with an HTML body** (not empty): `<TITLE>ERROR: The request could not be satisfied</TITLE> … <H1>403 ERROR</H1> Request blocked.` — itzg captured this and had to string-match the body because *"only the body seems to indicate the rate limit"* ([#2647](https://github.com/itzg/docker-minecraft-server/issues/2647)). So **empty body ⇒ auth, HTML body ⇒ throttle.** That distinction is your fastest triage.

### Things you asked about that I tested and **ruled out**

- **Cloudflare blocking datacenter IPs?** **No.** `api.curseforge.com` and the forgecdn hosts are **AWS CloudFront + Fastly/ioRiver/S3, not Cloudflare.** All CDN downloads from this datacenter IP returned 200. (`www.curseforge.com` — the *website* — *is* behind Cloudflare and *does* challenge this IP with a 403 "Just a moment…", so scraping the site from a server will fail. That's a separate surface.)
- **User-Agent required?** **No.** I fetched a real jar with `User-Agent:` empty, with the default curl UA, and with a browser UA — **all 200.** I found no documented UA requirement from Overwolf. Sending a descriptive UA is still good citizenship (Nexus formally requires it; CurseForge does not), but it is not the cause of your 403.

### 🚨 Time-sensitive: CDN downloads now require an API key

[CurseForge blog, "Introducing API Key Authentication for CurseForge File Downloads", Niv Hajaj, **Jun 10, 2026**](https://blog.curseforge.com/introducing-api-key-authentication-for-curseforge-file-downloads/) — verbatim:

> "We're rolling out API key authentication for direct file downloads from the CurseForge CDN (edge.forgecdn.net). If your application downloads files from CurseForge, this affects you."
>
> "This is aimed at the developers and operators of any tool or service that downloads files from the CurseForge CDN: **launchers, modpack installers, server tools, and similar integrations.**"
>
> "The endpoint itself stays the same: `https://edge.forgecdn.net/files/{id}/{subId}/{filename}`"
>
> "**Phase: Future (July 16th) — Behavior: API key required. Requests without a valid key return 401 Unauthorized.**"
>
> ```
> HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
> { "error": "Unauthorized", "message": "A valid api-key is required." }
> ```
>
> Two methods: `x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY` header (*"the preferred method for production"*) **or** `?api-key=YOUR_API_KEY` query param.
>
> "Build for this now: handle 401 responses gracefully and surface a clear, actionable message rather than failing silently."

**Observed reality as of today (2026-09-19, two months past the stated enforcement date): enforcement is NOT live.** Unauthenticated CDN downloads still return 200 from this datacenter IP, and a *bogus* `?api-key=` / `x-api-key` is also accepted (200). So the deadline slipped — but **build the key into your CDN fetch path now.** Note also that the blog says nothing about `allowModDistribution`; keying the CDN is about *attribution analytics*, and it gives CurseForge the switch to enforce the distribution toggle at the CDN too, which would break any manual-URL construction overnight.

### Is manual URL construction allowed?

It **works** (proven above), and CurseForge's own blog documents the URL shape. But nothing authorises using it to reach files the API declines to give you a `downloadUrl` for. Constructing a URL for an `allowModDistribution=false` mod is circumventing an access-control mechanism — see the "circumvent any security mechanisms" clause in (g). **Use `downloadUrl` from the File object (or `/download-url`) as the source of truth; only construct manually as a fallback for files the API already told you are distributable.**

## (f) Rate limits

**Nothing is documented.** I grepped the complete docs page for "rate", "limit", "quota", "throttle" — the only hits are legal boilerplate and the *pagination* limit. There are **no published request-rate figures and no rate-limit response headers**.

Community-observed behaviour:
- Throttling is enforced at **CloudFront**, returning **403 with an HTML "Request blocked" body**, not 429 with headers. From [itzg/docker-minecraft-server#2647](https://github.com/itzg/docker-minecraft-server/issues/2647): itzg — *"I grabbed a new capture and only the body seems to indicate the rate limit. I was previously looking only at the headers, since that's where APIs like Github's put rate limit information"*; a contributor — *"Can't find any rate limit headers in the response, its pretty weird to not send them there. Probably they just set a rate limit via cloudfront, guess we have to guess then."*
- itzg's own advice: *"I highly recommend you remove the `restart` policy parameter until you have your container setup initially. Otherwise, you will exceed the rate limit that CurseForge imposes."* — i.e. a crash-loop of a single container is enough to trip it.
- Reported reset window is roughly an hour.

**Engineering implication:** you must implement your own client-side token bucket + exponential backoff and treat *any* 403-with-HTML-body as a throttle signal. You get no headers to adapt from. Given the 10,000-result pagination cap plus undocumented throttling, a full catalog sync must be a slow, sharded, resumable background job — never on a customer's request path.

## (g) LEGAL — CurseForge / Overwolf

Three documents apply, in this order of specificity.

### 1. CurseForge 3rd Party API Terms and Conditions — **this is the one that governs you**
[support.curseforge.com/.../9000207405](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000207405-curseforge-3rd-party-api-terms-and-conditions) (modified 14 Aug 2024). Opens: *"PLEASE READ THIS AGREEMENT CAREFULLY; THIS IS A BINDING CONTRACT."* Governing law: **State of Israel, courts of Tel-Aviv.**

> "**'External App'** means any application created by Developer and using the Platform API and/or any SDK, **provided that such application provides substantial functionality above and beyond the functionality and materials provided through the Platform API and/or SDK.**"

**Licence grant** (verbatim):

## (b) 🚨 Is `download_link` premium-only? — **YES for unattended use. This is the decisive finding.**

Verbatim from the v1 spec description of `GET /v1/games/{game_domain_name}/mods/{mod_id}/files/{id}/download_link.json`:

> "Generate download link for mod file. **For premium users, will return array of download links with their prefered download location in the first element.**
>
> **NOTE: Non-premium members must provide the key and expiry from the .nxm link provided by the website. It is recommended for clients to extract them from the nxm link before sending this request. This ensures that all non-premium members must access the website to download through the API.**"

And the documented error responses, verbatim:

> - **`403`: "You don't have permission to get download links from the API without visting nexusmods.com - this is for premium users only."**
> - `400`: "Provided key and expire time isn't correct for this user/file."
> - `410`: "This link has expired - please visit the mod page again to get a new link."

**Read the design intent in that note: "This ensures that all non-premium members must access the website to download through the API."** The `key`/`expires` query params are not a workaround — they are the enforcement. They are minted by nexusmods.com when a logged-in human clicks the "Mod Manager Download" button, handed to the desktop client via the `nxm://` protocol handler, and they expire. There is no server-side, non-interactive way for a non-premium user's file to be fetched. A hosting control panel cannot manufacture them without either (a) the customer being Premium, or (b) driving a browser session on their behalf — which is separately prohibited (see (e)).

**Also checked and ruled out:** the v2 GraphQL `ModFile.uri` field is **just the filename**, not a URL. Live query for Unofficial Skyrim SE Patch returned `"uri":"Unofficial Skyrim Special Edition Patch-266-4-1-1.7z"`. There is no keyless download path.

## (c) Rate limits — ⚠️ **the two official sources disagree; the figures you have are the old ones**

**v1 spec** (verbatim):
> "We utilise user-based rate limiting on our API, so refreshing your API key (this can be done on the API Access page) will not allow you to exceed the rate limits. Our limits are as follows:
> > **2,500 requests within 24 hours and once this limit has been exceeded by a user they are then restricted to 100 requests per hour.**
>
> The API will return headers to inform the client of the remaining requests and remaining time:
> ```
> X-RL-Hourly-Limit     →100
> X-RL-Hourly-Remaining →96
> X-RL-Hourly-Reset     →2019-02-01T12:00:00+00:00
> X-RL-Daily-Limit      →2500
> X-RL-Daily-Remaining  →2488
> X-RL-Daily-Reset      →2019-02-02 00:00:00 +0000
> ```"

**Help centre article, last updated June 3, 2026** ([help.nexusmods.com/article/105](https://help.nexusmods.com/article/105-i-have-reached-a-daily-or-hourly-limit-api-requests-have-been-consumed-rate-limit-exceeded-what-does-this-mean)) — verbatim:
> "As a security measure, we limit user requests to our public API to a reasonable limit. **The limit is 20,000 requests per 24-hour period, and once that limit has been reached 500 requests per hour.**"
> "To put this into perspective, **Vortex consumes 3 requests per mod download**… meaning you could, in theory, download up to 6664 mods via Vortex… before reaching the 20,000 request limit."
> "**The daily quota resets for all users at 00:00 GMT each day. The hourly quota resets each hour.**"
> "**This information is sent in the response header to every request made to the API.**"

**Take the help-centre figures (20,000/day, 500/hour) as current** — it's dated 3 months ago vs. a spec whose header examples are timestamped 2019. Either way, the critical property is unchanged and fatal for your model: **the limit is per-USER, not per-application.** *"we utilise user-based rate limiting on our API, so refreshing your API key… will not allow you to exceed the rate limits."* Every request you make burns a real customer's personal quota — and the customer, not you, gets locked out of Vortex when it's exhausted.

## (d) GraphQL v2 — **live, powerful, unauthenticated, and entirely undocumented**

`https://api.nexusmods.com/v2/graphql` **exists and works with no API key at all.** I verified live:

```
POST /v2/graphql  {"query":"{ __typename }"}  → 200 {"data":{"__typename":"Query"}}
```

**Full introspection is open.** The Query root exposes 60+ fields, including `games`, `mods` (paged, filterable), `mod`, `modFiles`, `modsByUid`, `legacyModsByDomain`, `collections`, `collectionsV2`, `categories`, `tags`, `news`, `user`, `fileHash` ("Get Mod FileHash by md5"), `modEndorsers`, plus admin/moderation fields (`csamDeletionRequests`, `temporalWorkflowInspection`, `moderationWarnings`) that are clearly not meant for public consumption.

Real unauthenticated data query, executed successfully:
```graphql
{ mods(filter:{gameDomainName:{value:"skyrimspecialedition",op:EQUALS}}, count:2)
  { nodes { modId name summary downloads endorsements game{domainName} uploader{name} } } }
```
→ returned live mod records with names, summaries, uploaders.

Notable type fields discovered: **`Mod.directDownloadEnabled`** (Nexus's analogue of CurseForge's distribution toggle) with a corresponding `Mutation.updateModDirectDownloadEnabled`; `ModMirror.uri`; `ModFile.uri` (filename only); `CollectionRevision.downloadLink`.

**What is known/public:** essentially nothing official. It is not in `api-docs.nexusmods.com` (which documents v3), not on SwaggerHub (v1), and [modding.wiki/en/nexusmods/api](https://www.modding.wiki/en/nexusmods/api) says only *"API documentation is coming soon."* It is the internal backend for nexusmods.com, the Nexus Mods App and Collections. **Treat it as unsupported and unstable — and note that using it is squarely "scraping" under the AUP.** Building a catalog on it would be the most technically capable and the most legally exposed option available.

## (f) Practical verdict on Nexus — **NO. Unambiguously no.**

Nexus Mods is **not usable** as a source for a commercial hosting platform's auto-installer. This is not a grey area; it fails on four independent grounds, each individually disqualifying, and each stated in Nexus's own words:

1. **The installer itself is a named prohibited use.** — *"Storing user API keys on your own server and/or using them without the action being initiated by the user."* ([AUP](https://help.nexusmods.com/article/114-api-acceptable-use-policy)) A server-side auto-installer is exactly this.
2. **The catalog itself is a named prohibited use.** — *"Fetching data en-masse with the intent to rehost this information on your own service (i.e. scraping)."* ([AUP](https://help.nexusmods.com/article/114-api-acceptable-use-policy)) Reinforced by ToS §11: *"You shall not conduct, facilitate, authorise or permit any text or data mining or web scraping… for any purpose."*
3. **Commercial use requires a licence you don't have.** — *"You must not use any part of the content on our site for commercial purposes without obtaining a licence to do so from us or our licensors."* (ToS §10) And downloads are permitted *"for your own personal use"* only.
4. **The download mechanism is deliberately engineered to prevent it.** — *"This ensures that all non-premium members must access the website to download through the API"*, backed by `403: "You don't have permission to get download links from the API without visting nexusmods.com - this is for premium users only."* ([v1 spec](https://app.swaggerhub.com/apis-docs/NexusMods/nexus-mods_public_api_params_in_form_data/1.0)) Plus per-user rate limits that make *your* traffic exhaust *your customer's* quota.

There is no "ask nicely and get a licence" path worth pursuing here either: registration is discretionary (*"We reserve the right to deny registration… with or without providing a reason"*), favours open-source apps, and the whole policy is framed around *"the benefit of the modding community"* rather than commercial resale.

**Recommendation:** drop Nexus from the auto-installer scope entirely. If you want to serve Nexus-modded games (Skyrim, Fallout, Stardew, Valheim, etc.), the only defensible design is **link-out plus customer upload**: deep-link the customer to the mod page on nexusmods.com (permitted under §27 if you don't imply endorsement), let them download it themselves under their own account and licence, and give them a clean SFTP/web-upload path into their server. That keeps the download "initiated by the user", under the user's own account, at the user's own quota — and it is honest with the customer about where the file came from.

# Cross-cutting recommendations

**CurseForge is the viable source — conditionally.** Modrinth (not researched here, but the obvious third leg) is the genuinely permissive option and should be your primary; CurseForge second, with an approved key; Nexus link-out only.

**Before writing installer code, get three things in writing from Overwolf** as part of the key application — all three are real blockers, not formalities:
1. **Permission to cache API data.** The literal terms say *"save or cache any data obtained through the API or SDK"* is prohibited. Your catalog cannot exist without caching. Ask explicitly.
2. **Confirmation you are not a "competitor."** *"shall not… build any product or service that competes, directly or indirectly, with CF, CurseForge for Studios, or the Platform."* A hosting company shipping a mod browser is arguable. Get it acknowledged.
3. **A rate-limit/quota figure.** Nothing is published; the terms let Overwolf impose a paid licensing agreement above an undisclosed quota. Ask what the quota is before you build capacity assumptions on it.

**Three engineering constraints to design around from day one:**
- **Persist and refresh `allowModDistribution`**; badge or hide blocked mods in the catalog rather than failing at install. Ship the manual-upload fallback in v1, not v2 — every comparable tool needed it.
- **Add `x-api-key` to CDN fetches now.** Enforcement was announced for 2026-07-16 and has slipped, but it will land, and the failure mode is a hard 401 on every install.
- **Build your own throttle.** CurseForge returns no rate-limit headers; a 403 with an HTML body means throttled, a 403 with an empty body means bad key. Catalog sync must be a sharded, resumable background job — the 10,000-result pagination cap means you cannot enumerate any large category in one pass.

**Fix the current 403 first** — check the API key's byte length at the point of use. Bcrypt-shaped keys (`$2a$10$…`) get silently truncated by shell and Docker Compose `$`-expansion, and that single cause accounts for most reported CurseForge 403s.

**Two things I could not verify:** whether CurseForge keys carry any monetary cost at the tier you'd need (no pricing is published anywhere; the terms only say a written licensing agreement "may contain payment requirements" above an undisclosed quota), and the current console.curseforge.com signup flow (it's a JS app I couldn't drive). Both need a human to walk the console and the application form.</result>

# PART 1 — CurseForge ("Eternal") API

## (a) Base URL, auth, keys, gates

**Base URL** — verbatim from the docs: *"All endpoints use the same base URL - `https://api.curseforge.com`"* ([docs.curseforge.com/rest-api](https://docs.curseforge.com/rest-api/))

**Auth header** — verbatim: *"API Key (API_KEY) — Parameter Name: `x-api-key`, in: header. The API key can be generated in the CurseForge for Studios developer console."* (same page). Every endpoint ends with *"To perform this operation, you must be authenticated by means of one of the following methods: API_KEY"*.

**How to get a key** — [console.curseforge.com](https://console.curseforge.com/) (SPA; I could only confirm it loads, not walk its UI). The gating is described verbatim in the support article ([support.curseforge.com/.../9000208346](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000208346-about-the-curseforge-api-and-how-to-apply-for-a-key), modified 3 Dec 2024):

> "We're going to use the commonly used API system, which means API access will be granted to each requester as a unique key which can be generated after 3rd party developers submit an application. This can be done through a form and reviewed by the Overwolf team. The form covers contact information, project description, links and coursed, expected API use etc. To complete the form also requires approving the 3rd Party Developers API Terms of Service. Upon Overwolf review and approval, the unique key will be generated and the developer will be contacted via email."

And the review criteria, verbatim:

> "What will our team look for in the application? — How it impacts on Authors' earnings / How it affects CurseForge's servers and CDN / How it takes Authors' consent when it comes to third party distribution of their creations"

**Is it free?** No price is stated anywhere I could find. But the 3rd Party API Terms contain a commercial trigger, verbatim:

> "Upon the External App exceeding a certain quota, to be decided and updated from time to time upon Overwolf's sole discretion, continued use of the Platform API and/or SDK may (at Overwolf's sole discretion) require Developer to enter into a written licensing agreement with Overwolf, which license agreement may contain payment requirements or other terms and conditions applicable to the continued use of the API or SDK." ([3rd Party API T&C](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000207405-curseforge-3rd-party-api-terms-and-conditions))

**Could not verify:** an earlier automated read of the docs quoted *"Not a game developer? If you're running a 3rd party modding service, we have an API solution for you"* and *"Any registered account which is not a game developer and did not request a key, will be deleted."* I downloaded the raw HTML of `docs.curseforge.com/rest-api/` (1.1 MB) and **neither string is present**. Treat those as stale/unverified.

**Keys are game-scoped.** `GET /v1/games` is documented as *"Get all games that are available to the provided API key."* — relevant to 403s (see (e)).

## (c) Mod object fields — and the license question

This can be false when a mod is experimental, in a deleted state or has only alpha files"*), `thumbsUpCount`, `rating` (nullable decimal).

`File` object: `id`, `gameId`, `modId`, `isAvailable` (*"Whether the file is available to download"*), `displayName`, `fileName`, `releaseType`, `fileStatus`, `hashes[]` (md5/sha1), `fileDate`, `fileLength`, `downloadCount`, `fileSizeOnDisk`, **`downloadUrl`** (*"The file download URL"*), `gameVersions[]`, `sortableGameVersions[]`, `dependencies[]` (`modId` + `relationType`), `exposeAsAlternative`, `parentProjectFileId`, `alternateFileId`, **`isServerPack`**, **`serverPackFileId`**, `isEarlyAccessContent`, `earlyAccessEndDate`, `fileFingerprint`, `modules[]`.

> `isServerPack` / `serverPackFileId` are the two fields that matter most for a hosting installer — many Minecraft modpacks ship a distinct server-side pack file.

### License: confirmed — **the CurseForge API does NOT expose a license field.** ✅

I grepped the entire rendered docs page (211 KB of text, every schema and every example response). The word "license" appears exactly **4 times**, all inside the *CurseForge for Studios Terms of Use* legal boilerplate ("non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide license to the name, logo and trademarks…"). It appears in **zero** schema definitions. There is no `license`, `licenseType`, `licenseUrl`, or `licenseName` on `Mod`, `File`, or any other object.

Corroborating evidence: [cfwidget.com](https://cfwidget.com/), the long-standing third-party CurseForge proxy, still has a `license` key in its JSON but it is **empty for every project I tested** — JEI, JourneyMap, Applied Energistics 2, Iron Chests, Create all return `"license": ""` (tested live against `api.cfwidget.com`).

**Where license lives instead:** on the CurseForge *website*, on the project's **License tab** (author-editable) and rendered in the project page's About panel. The support article on the distribution toggle says, verbatim: *"Simply click the 'Go to License Tab' button and you'll be transferred to the relevant tab… You can also edit this toggle by entering the project page > 'License tab'."* and *"Only project owners and members with the 'license' permission enabled can view the License tab"* ([Project Distribution Toggle](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000207877-project-distribution-toggle)).

**Practical consequence for you:** you cannot build a license-filtered catalog from the API. Getting license text means scraping `www.curseforge.com` — which is **explicitly prohibited** (see (g)) and technically blocked (I got `HTTP 403 "Just a moment… Enable JavaScript and cookies to continue"` — Cloudflare challenge — on both `curseforge.com/legal/terms` and `curseforge.com/terms/mod-author` from this server).

## (d) The `allowModDistribution=false` / `downloadUrl=null` problem

**What it is.** Authors can flip a per-project switch. Verbatim from CurseForge ([Project Distribution Toggle](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000207877-project-distribution-toggle)):

> "The project distribution toggle is all about providing authors control over their intellectual property and revenue generated from their awesome creations. The toggle is part of the new CurseForge API, and determines if 3rd party developers can or cannot distribute your project information and files."
>
> "If you turn this option off **Any 3rd-party service, website or client will not have access to your projects or files via the 3rd-party API.**"
>
> "If you turn this option on any download from the 3rd party service **will not count towards your total downloads nor towards your Reward Program earnings.**"
>
> "As a default, all existing projects have the option toggled on and allow distribution."
>
> **"We recommend choosing a license preference that is compatible with your distribution choice. In any case - the API will respect the toggle choice over the license type choice."**

That last sentence is the one to internalise: **an MIT- or LGPL-licensed mod can still have `allowModDistribution=false`, and CurseForge will enforce the toggle over the licence.** The open licence may give you the legal right to redistribute, but CurseForge will not serve you the bytes through the API.

**Mechanically**, `Mod.allowModDistribution=false` ⇒ `File.downloadUrl` comes back `null` and `/download-url` fails. The API returns full metadata but no file.

**How widespread?** No official statistic exists — I searched and could not find one, and CurseForge has never published a number. Only anecdotes, and they cut both ways:
- All the Mods 9 (a ~400-mod pack): 3 mods blocked.
- A 114-mod pack: 4 blocked ([xenodeve/minecraft-100day#80](https://github.com/xenodeve/minecraft-100day/issues/80)).
- Individual high-traffic libraries have been the pain point — e.g. long-running author requests on [architectury/architectury-api#262](https://github.com/architectury/architectury-api/issues/262), [EccentricVamp/EccentricTome#18](https://github.com/EccentricVamp/EccentricTome/issues/18), [Flemmli97/TenshiLib#8](https://github.com/Flemmli97/TenshiLib/issues/8), [mrsterner/GuardVillagers#23](https://github.com/mrsterner/GuardVillagers/issues/23), [r8420/MoreOverlays-updated#62](https://github.com/r8420/MoreOverlays-updated/issues/62).

**Realistic read: low single-digit percent of projects, but non-uniformly distributed** — it clusters on libraries and popular mods, so the probability that *a given modpack* contains at least one blocked mod is high. For your use case that is what matters: a 1–3% per-mod block rate is a ~50%+ per-pack failure rate.

**What third-party launchers actually do — they all give up and hand it to the human:**
- **Prism Launcher**: on a blocked mod the pack install halts and the user is given a link list; Prism then watches the Downloads folder and copies files into place. Tracked as bugs because the UX is bad: [#599 "Attempting to download mods from CurseForge that have 3rd party downloads disabled results in undetermined behavior"](https://github.com/PrismLauncher/PrismLauncher/issues/599) (version dropdown shows *"No valid version found!"*; downloads fail silently and the mod appears installed but isn't), [#3220](https://github.com/PrismLauncher/PrismLauncher/issues/3220), [#3844](https://github.com/PrismLauncher/PrismLauncher/issues/3844).
- **itzg/docker-minecraft-server** (the de-facto standard Minecraft server image, i.e. your closest analogue): verbatim from its docs — *"For mod, modpacks, and world files that are not allowed for automated download, the container path `/downloads` can be attached and matching files will be retrieved from there."* and *"It's important to use a browser to download the files listed for manual download."* ([auto-curseforge docs](https://docker-minecraft-server.readthedocs.io/en/latest/types-and-platforms/mod-platforms/auto-curseforge/))
- **Modrinth** deliberately does not integrate: *"some of them, like CurseForge, are Modrinth's competitors. They won't allow the use of their APIs to Modrinth, or if they do, it would be under a contract with terms that might make experience worse for Modrinth users."* ([modrinth/code#3631](https://github.com/modrinth/code/issues/3631))

**What it means for a hosting company.** You cannot promise "one-click install for any CurseForge mod." You must:
1. Store `allowModDistribution` per mod, refresh it (authors flip it), and **exclude or clearly badge blocked mods in your catalog UI** rather than failing at install time.
2. Provide an upload/SFTP fallback path for blocked mods — that is what every serious tool does, and it is also the honest answer to give customers.
3. Never construct a CDN URL to bypass the flag. Doing so circumvents an access-control mechanism, which is a named prohibited act in the API terms (see (g)) and voids the author consent that CurseForge's whole approval process is built around.

**Historical context**: the toggle shipped alongside the official API on 16 May 2022, which broke MultiMC/PolyMC/GDLauncher/PCL2 modpack installs. CurseForge's rationale, as reported: downloads from 3rd-party services rely on CurseForge servers and CDN, incurring costs and bypassing the monetization that funds the Author Rewards program.

## (e) CDN URL pattern, manual construction, and your 403 — **I reproduced this live**

### The URL scheme (empirically verified today from this server)

`edge.forgecdn.net` is a CloudFront distribution that **302-redirects** to `mediafilez.forgecdn.net` (Fastly/ioRiver in front of an S3 bucket). Observed:

```
GET https://edge.forgecdn.net/files/8911/160/jei-26.3-neoforge-31.0.0.7.jar
→ HTTP/2 302, location: https://mediafilez.forgecdn.net/files/8911/160/...
   (via CloudFront, x-amz-cf-pop: SIN3-P4)
→ HTTP/2 200, 1,905,807 bytes, content-type: application/java-archive
   (server: AmazonS3, x-ioriver: Fastly)
```

**The exact fileId → path rule (I tested all four variants):**

```
https://mediafilez.forgecdn.net/files/{floor(fileId/1000)}/{fileId % 1000}/{fileName}
```

| Tested path | Result |
|---|---|
| `/files/8911/160/jei-26.3-neoforge-31.0.0.7.jar` (id 8911160) | **200**, 1905807 B |
| `/files/8880/75/jei-26.2-neoforge-30.32.0.220.jar` (id 8880**075**) | **200**, 1919971 B |
| `/files/8880/**075**/…` (zero-padded) | **403** |
| `/files/8851/9/jei-1.20.1-forge-15.59.0.210.jar` (id 8851**009**) | **200**, 1825651 B |
| `/files/8851/**009**/…` (zero-padded) | **403** |

⚠️ **The second segment is NOT zero-padded.** This is the classic bug: fileId `8851009` → `8851/9`, not `8851/009`. Padding gives a 403. (Note the community shorthand *"the file id is segmented every four digits"* from [Coadon/CurseFetch](https://github.com/Coadon/CurseFetch) is a rough approximation that breaks on these cases — use `divmod(fileId, 1000)`.)

### Your 403 with empty body — diagnosed

**It is almost certainly `api.curseforge.com`, not the CDN.** I reproduced it exactly:

```
$ curl -D - https://api.curseforge.com/v1/games            # no key
HTTP/2 403
content-length: 0
x-cache: Error from cloudfront

$ curl -H "x-api-key: notarealkey" https://api.curseforge.com/v1/games
HTTP/2 403   (empty body)
```

**403 + `content-length: 0` + `x-cache: Error from cloudfront` is CloudFront rejecting the API key at the edge before your request reaches the app.** Causes, in order of likelihood:

1. **Key mangled by shell/env interpolation.** CurseForge keys are bcrypt-shaped (`$2a$10$…`). `$2a`, `$10` get eaten by shell `$`-expansion / Docker Compose variable substitution, silently truncating the key. This is by far the most-reported cause: [itzg/docker-minecraft-server#3591 "Access to CurseForge API is forbidden despite valid CF_API_KEY"](https://github.com/itzg/docker-minecraft-server/issues/3591) — the fix is no quotes in `.env`, or `$$` doubling in Compose. Check the key's exact byte length at the point of use.
2. **Key not authorised for that game.** Docs: *"Get all games that are available to the provided API key."* Keys are scoped; a Studios/game-developer key will 403 on Minecraft data.
3. **Rate limited.** When throttled, CloudFront returns a **403 with an HTML body** (not empty): `<TITLE>ERROR: The request could not be satisfied</TITLE> … <H1>403 ERROR</H1> Request blocked.` — itzg captured this and had to string-match the body because *"only the body seems to indicate the rate limit"* ([#2647](https://github.com/itzg/docker-minecraft-server/issues/2647)). So **empty body ⇒ auth, HTML body ⇒ throttle.** That distinction is your fastest triage.

### Things you asked about that I tested and **ruled out**

- **Cloudflare blocking datacenter IPs?** **No.** `api.curseforge.com` and the forgecdn hosts are **AWS CloudFront + Fastly/ioRiver/S3, not Cloudflare.** All CDN downloads from this datacenter IP returned 200. (`www.curseforge.com` — the *website* — *is* behind Cloudflare and *does* challenge this IP with a 403 "Just a moment…", so scraping the site from a server will fail. That's a separate surface.)
- **User-Agent required?** **No.** I fetched a real jar with `User-Agent:` empty, with the default curl UA, and with a browser UA — **all 200.** I found no documented UA requirement from Overwolf. Sending a descriptive UA is still good citizenship (Nexus formally requires it; CurseForge does not), but it is not the cause of your 403.

### 🚨 Time-sensitive: CDN downloads now require an API key

[CurseForge blog, "Introducing API Key Authentication for CurseForge File Downloads", Niv Hajaj, **Jun 10, 2026**](https://blog.curseforge.com/introducing-api-key-authentication-for-curseforge-file-downloads/) — verbatim:

> "We're rolling out API key authentication for direct file downloads from the CurseForge CDN (edge.forgecdn.net). If your application downloads files from CurseForge, this affects you."
>
> "This is aimed at the developers and operators of any tool or service that downloads files from the CurseForge CDN: **launchers, modpack installers, server tools, and similar integrations.**"
>
> "The endpoint itself stays the same: `https://edge.forgecdn.net/files/{id}/{subId}/{filename}`"
>
> "**Phase: Future (July 16th) — Behavior: API key required. Requests without a valid key return 401 Unauthorized.**"
>
> ```
> HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
> { "error": "Unauthorized", "message": "A valid api-key is required." }
> ```
>
> Two methods: `x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY` header (*"the preferred method for production"*) **or** `?api-key=YOUR_API_KEY` query param.
>
> "Build for this now: handle 401 responses gracefully and surface a clear, actionable message rather than failing silently."

**Observed reality as of today (2026-09-19, two months past the stated enforcement date): enforcement is NOT live.** Unauthenticated CDN downloads still return 200 from this datacenter IP, and a *bogus* `?api-key=` / `x-api-key` is also accepted (200). So the deadline slipped — but **build the key into your CDN fetch path now.** Note also that the blog says nothing about `allowModDistribution`; keying the CDN is about *attribution analytics*, and it gives CurseForge the switch to enforce the distribution toggle at the CDN too, which would break any manual-URL construction overnight.

### Is manual URL construction allowed?

It **works** (proven above), and CurseForge's own blog documents the URL shape. But nothing authorises using it to reach files the API declines to give you a `downloadUrl` for. Constructing a URL for an `allowModDistribution=false` mod is circumventing an access-control mechanism — see the "circumvent any security mechanisms" clause in (g). **Use `downloadUrl` from the File object (or `/download-url`) as the source of truth; only construct manually as a fallback for files the API already told you are distributable.**

## (f) Rate limits

**Nothing is documented.** I grepped the complete docs page for "rate", "limit", "quota", "throttle" — the only hits are legal boilerplate and the *pagination* limit. There are **no published request-rate figures and no rate-limit response headers**.

Community-observed behaviour:
- Throttling is enforced at **CloudFront**, returning **403 with an HTML "Request blocked" body**, not 429 with headers. From [itzg/docker-minecraft-server#2647](https://github.com/itzg/docker-minecraft-server/issues/2647): itzg — *"I grabbed a new capture and only the body seems to indicate the rate limit. I was previously looking only at the headers, since that's where APIs like Github's put rate limit information"*; a contributor — *"Can't find any rate limit headers in the response, its pretty weird to not send them there. Probably they just set a rate limit via cloudfront, guess we have to guess then."*
- itzg's own advice: *"I highly recommend you remove the `restart` policy parameter until you have your container setup initially. Otherwise, you will exceed the rate limit that CurseForge imposes."* — i.e. a crash-loop of a single container is enough to trip it.
- Reported reset window is roughly an hour.

**Engineering implication:** you must implement your own client-side token bucket + exponential backoff and treat *any* 403-with-HTML-body as a throttle signal. You get no headers to adapt from. Given the 10,000-result pagination cap plus undocumented throttling, a full catalog sync must be a slow, sharded, resumable background job — never on a customer's request path.

## (g) LEGAL — CurseForge / Overwolf

Three documents apply, in this order of specificity.

### 1. CurseForge 3rd Party API Terms and Conditions — **this is the one that governs you**
[support.curseforge.com/.../9000207405](https://support.curseforge.com/support/solutions/articles/9000207405-curseforge-3rd-party-api-terms-and-conditions) (modified 14 Aug 2024). Opens: *"PLEASE READ THIS AGREEMENT CAREFULLY; THIS IS A BINDING CONTRACT."* Governing law: **State of Israel, courts of Tel-Aviv.**

**Definition of what you're allowed to build** (verbatim):
> "**'External App'** means any application created by Developer and using the Platform API and/or any SDK, **provided that such application provides substantial functionality above and beyond the functionality and materials provided through the Platform API and/or SDK.**"

**Licence grant** (verbatim):
> "Overwolf shall allow Developer during the term of these Terms the non-exclusive right to use the Platform API solely in order to create applications that are External Apps."

## (b) 🚨 Is `download_link` premium-only? — **YES for unattended use. This is the decisive finding.**

Verbatim from the v1 spec description of `GET /v1/games/{game_domain_name}/mods/{mod_id}/files/{id}/download_link.json`:

> "Generate download link for mod file. **For premium users, will return array of download links with their prefered download location in the first element.**
>
> **NOTE: Non-premium members must provide the key and expiry from the .nxm link provided by the website. It is recommended for clients to extract them from the nxm link before sending this request. This ensures that all non-premium members must access the website to download through the API.**"

And the documented error responses, verbatim:

> - **`403`: "You don't have permission to get download links from the API without visting nexusmods.com - this is for premium users only."**
> - `400`: "Provided key and expire time isn't correct for this user/file."
> - `410`: "This link has expired - please visit the mod page again to get a new link."

**Read the design intent in that note: "This ensures that all non-premium members must access the website to download through the API."** The `key`/`expires` query params are not a workaround — they are the enforcement. They are minted by nexusmods.com when a logged-in human clicks the "Mod Manager Download" button, handed to the desktop client via the `nxm://` protocol handler, and they expire. There is no server-side, non-interactive way for a non-premium user's file to be fetched. A hosting control panel cannot manufacture them without either (a) the customer being Premium, or (b) driving a browser session on their behalf — which is separately prohibited (see (e)).

**Also checked and ruled out:** the v2 GraphQL `ModFile.uri` field is **just the filename**, not a URL. Live query for Unofficial Skyrim SE Patch returned `"uri":"Unofficial Skyrim Special Edition Patch-266-4-1-1.7z"`. There is no keyless download path.

## (c) Rate limits — ⚠️ **the two official sources disagree; the figures you have are the old ones**

**v1 spec** (verbatim):
> "We utilise user-based rate limiting on our API, so refreshing your API key (this can be done on the API Access page) will not allow you to exceed the rate limits. Our limits are as follows:
> > **2,500 requests within 24 hours and once this limit has been exceeded by a user they are then restricted to 100 requests per hour.**
>
> The API will return headers to inform the client of the remaining requests and remaining time:
> ```
> X-RL-Hourly-Limit     →100
> X-RL-Hourly-Remaining →96
> X-RL-Hourly-Reset     →2019-02-01T12:00:00+00:00
> X-RL-Daily-Limit      →2500
> X-RL-Daily-Remaining  →2488
> X-RL-Daily-Reset      →2019-02-02 00:00:00 +0000
> ```"

**Help centre article, last updated June 3, 2026** ([help.nexusmods.com/article/105](https://help.nexusmods.com/article/105-i-have-reached-a-daily-or-hourly-limit-api-requests-have-been-consumed-rate-limit-exceeded-what-does-this-mean)) — verbatim:
> "As a security measure, we limit user requests to our public API to a reasonable limit. **The limit is 20,000 requests per 24-hour period, and once that limit has been reached 500 requests per hour.**"
> "To put this into perspective, **Vortex consumes 3 requests per mod download**… meaning you could, in theory, download up to 6664 mods via Vortex… before reaching the 20,000 request limit."
> "**The daily quota resets for all users at 00:00 GMT each day. The hourly quota resets each hour.**"
> "**This information is sent in the response header to every request made to the API.**"

**Take the help-centre figures (20,000/day, 500/hour) as current** — it's dated 3 months ago vs. a spec whose header examples are timestamped 2019. Either way, the critical property is unchanged and fatal for your model: **the limit is per-USER, not per-application.** *"we utilise user-based rate limiting on our API, so refreshing your API key… will not allow you to exceed the rate limits."* Every request you make burns a real customer's personal quota — and the customer, not you, gets locked out of Vortex when it's exhausted.

## (d) GraphQL v2 — **live, powerful, unauthenticated, and entirely undocumented**

`https://api.nexusmods.com/v2/graphql` **exists and works with no API key at all.** I verified live:

```
POST /v2/graphql  {"query":"{ __typename }"}  → 200 {"data":{"__typename":"Query"}}
```

**Full introspection is open.** The Query root exposes 60+ fields, including `games`, `mods` (paged, filterable), `mod`, `modFiles`, `modsByUid`, `legacyModsByDomain`, `collections`, `collectionsV2`, `categories`, `tags`, `news`, `user`, `fileHash` ("Get Mod FileHash by md5"), `modEndorsers`, plus admin/moderation fields (`csamDeletionRequests`, `temporalWorkflowInspection`, `moderationWarnings`) that are clearly not meant for public consumption.

Real unauthenticated data query, executed successfully:
```graphql
{ mods(filter:{gameDomainName:{value:"skyrimspecialedition",op:EQUALS}}, count:2)
  { nodes { modId name summary downloads endorsements game{domainName} uploader{name} } } }
```
→ returned live mod records with names, summaries, uploaders.

Notable type fields discovered: **`Mod.directDownloadEnabled`** (Nexus's analogue of CurseForge's distribution toggle) with a corresponding `Mutation.updateModDirectDownloadEnabled`; `ModMirror.uri`; `ModFile.uri` (filename only); `CollectionRevision.downloadLink`.

**What is known/public:** essentially nothing official. It is not in `api-docs.nexusmods.com` (which documents v3), not on SwaggerHub (v1), and [modding.wiki/en/nexusmods/api](https://www.modding.wiki/en/nexusmods/api) says only *"API documentation is coming soon."* It is the internal backend for nexusmods.com, the Nexus Mods App and Collections. **Treat it as unsupported and unstable — and note that using it is squarely "scraping" under the AUP.** Building a catalog on it would be the most technically capable and the most legally exposed option available.

## (f) Practical verdict on Nexus — **NO. Unambiguously no.**

Nexus Mods is **not usable** as a source for a commercial hosting platform's auto-installer. This is not a grey area; it fails on four independent grounds, each individually disqualifying, and each stated in Nexus's own words:

1. **The installer itself is a named prohibited use.** — *"Storing user API keys on your own server and/or using them without the action being initiated by the user."* ([AUP](https://help.nexusmods.com/article/114-api-acceptable-use-policy)) A server-side auto-installer is exactly this.
2. **The catalog itself is a named prohibited use.** — *"Fetching data en-masse with the intent to rehost this information on your own service (i.e. scraping)."* ([AUP](https://help.nexusmods.com/article/114-api-acceptable-use-policy)) Reinforced by ToS §11: *"You shall not conduct, facilitate, authorise or permit any text or data mining or web scraping… for any purpose."*
3. **Commercial use requires a licence you don't have.** — *"You must not use any part of the content on our site for commercial purposes without obtaining a licence to do so from us or our licensors."* (ToS §10) And downloads are permitted *"for your own personal use"* only.
4. **The download mechanism is deliberately engineered to prevent it.** — *"This ensures that all non-premium members must access the website to download through the API"*, backed by `403: "You don't have permission to get download links from the API without visting nexusmods.com - this is for premium users only."* ([v1 spec](https://app.swaggerhub.com/apis-docs/NexusMods/nexus-mods_public_api_params_in_form_data/1.0)) Plus per-user rate limits that make *your* traffic exhaust *your customer's* quota.

There is no "ask nicely and get a licence" path worth pursuing here either: registration is discretionary (*"We reserve the right to deny registration… with or without providing a reason"*), favours open-source apps, and the whole policy is framed around *"the benefit of the modding community"* rather than commercial resale.

**Recommendation:** drop Nexus from the auto-installer scope entirely. If you want to serve Nexus-modded games (Skyrim, Fallout, Stardew, Valheim, etc.), the only defensible design is **link-out plus customer upload**: deep-link the customer to the mod page on nexusmods.com (permitted under §27 if you don't imply endorsement), let them download it themselves under their own account and licence, and give them a clean SFTP/web-upload path into their server. That keeps the download "initiated by the user", under the user's own account, at the user's own quota — and it is honest with the customer about where the file came from.

# Cross-cutting recommendations

**CurseForge is the viable source — conditionally.** Modrinth (not researched here, but the obvious third leg) is the genuinely permissive option and should be your primary; CurseForge second, with an approved key; Nexus link-out only.

**Before writing installer code, get three things in writing from Overwolf** as part of the key application — all three are real blockers, not formalities:
1. **Permission to cache API data.** The literal terms say *"save or cache any data obtained through the API or SDK"* is prohibited. Your catalog cannot exist without caching. Ask explicitly.
2. **Confirmation you are not a "competitor."** *"shall not… build any product or service that competes, directly or indirectly, with CF, CurseForge for Studios, or the Platform."* A hosting company shipping a mod browser is arguable. Get it acknowledged.
3. **A rate-limit/quota figure.** Nothing is published; the terms let Overwolf impose a paid licensing agreement above an undisclosed quota. Ask what the quota is before you build capacity assumptions on it.

**Three engineering constraints to design around from day one:**
- **Persist and refresh `allowModDistribution`**; badge or hide blocked mods in the catalog rather than failing at install. Ship the manual-upload fallback in v1, not v2 — every comparable tool needed it.
- **Add `x-api-key` to CDN fetches now.** Enforcement was announced for 2026-07-16 and has slipped, but it will land, and the failure mode is a hard 401 on every install.
- **Build your own throttle.** CurseForge returns no rate-limit headers; a 403 with an HTML body means throttled, a 403 with an empty body means bad key. Catalog sync must be a sharded, resumable background job — the 10,000-result pagination cap means you cannot enumerate any large category in one pass.

**Fix the current 403 first** — check the API key's byte length at the point of use. Bcrypt-shaped keys (`$2a$10$…`) get silently truncated by shell and Docker Compose `$`-expansion, and that single cause accounts for most reported CurseForge 403s.

**Two things I could not verify:** whether CurseForge keys carry any monetary cost at the tier you'd need (no pricing is published anywhere; the terms only say a written licensing agreement "may contain payment requirements" above an undisclosed quota), and the current console.curseforge.com signup flow (it's a JS app I couldn't drive). Both need a human to walk the console and the application form.</result>
